strengths: The core idea is simple and well-motivated: clustering clients on the full vector of losses across K models (rather than the single lowest-loss model as in IFCA) is a natural relaxation that removes the need for careful near-optimal initialization, and Figure 1 provides a clear illustration of why IFCA can fail.

The theoretical analysis for the mixed linear regression setting is reasonably developed (Appendix A): it establishes separation of SLV cluster means (Lemmas A.1-A.2), concentration of SLVs (Lemma A.4), an operator-norm bound on centered SLVs (Lemma A.7), and one-shot cluster recovery via the proximity condition of [17] (Theorems A.9/A.10), plus exponential convergence of the models (Theorem 4.2). Lemma A.17 showing that IFCA's recovery condition implies loss-vector separation helps position the contribution against the closest baseline.

The empirical evaluation is broad: five datasets spanning image classification, text classification, and image reconstruction; four non-IID partitioning schemes; several CFL baselines (IFCA, FlexCFL, FeSEM, CFL, PACFL) and PFL baselines; ARI metrics; convergence-speed metrics; ablation studies; initialization-robustness experiments; and comparisons with k-FED on mixed linear regression.
The paper addresses both supervised and unsupervised settings with the same loss-based mechanism, which is a genuine advantage over many PFL methods that require labels.

The appendix reports additional skews (Tables 7-9), text-task details (Tables 10-11), personalization benefit heatmaps (Fig. 4), client-scaling and averaging-variant experiments, and compute/model details, which supports reproducibility of the evaluation.
weaknesses: Communication and computation overhead of the method is not analyzed or measured. CLoVE requires each participating client to run its data through all K models and the server to broadcast all K models every round, a K-fold increase over FedAvg/IFCA-style communication per round; this cost is nowhere quantified or discussed as a limitation, despite being a major practical consideration in FL.

The privacy treatment is dismissive. Sending raw loss vectors over all clients' local data to the server every round reveals substantially more than the paper acknowledges (loss magnitudes across K models on each client's dataset can leak information about label distribution, dataset size effects, etc.). The single-sentence claim that loss vectors reveal 'nothing about their data' is unsupported; no threat model, no differential privacy consideration, no empirical leakage analysis.

Some headline claims overstate the results. 'CLoVE is the only algorithm that consistently ranks among the top performers in almost all scenarios' is not fully supported: e.g., on CIFAR-10 under concept shift FedAvg achieves 63.1 vs CLoVE's 58.4, and on AG News FlexCFL achieves 60.2 vs CLoVE's 55.1. ARI=1.00 for FlexCFL in several settings matches CLoVE. The contributions bullet claims 'state-of-the-art model accuracy,' which is not uniformly true in the tables.

The theoretical guarantees are limited to a linear/mixed-linear-regression setting with fairly strong assumptions: unit-norm optimal models with minimum separation Δ close to 1, orthonormal or Δ-proximal initialization, K << M, K << d, n·m_k(ρ/(ρ+1))^2 >> polylog(K), and equal per-cluster sample sizes. There is a gap between these conditions and the deep-network experiments where no theory applies; the paper does not clearly delineate this gap.

The number of clusters K must be known in advance (an input to Algorithm 1), and the paper does not discuss sensitivity to misspecification of K, which most competing CFL methods also face but which should be addressed for completeness.

Only 3 random seeds are used per experiment, and differences of 1-3 points in the tables (e.g., CLoVE 97.1 vs FlexCFL 95.6 on MNIST label skew 2) may not be statistically meaningful given the reported standard deviations; the claimed wins are sometimes within noise.
The paper's own implementation (CLoVE) is marked 'self-implemented' with no GitHub link (Table 6 gives links only for baselines), which weakens reproducibility of the central method.

Unsupervised evaluation is thin: the only unsupervised CFL baseline compared is IFCA (Table 5, Fig. 2), and the unsupervised reconstruction-loss differences (e.g., 0.014 vs 0.019 on MNIST) are reported without significance analysis.

The comparison to [32] (Vardhan et al., improved IFCA) is dismissive ('but their methods are complex') and that method is not included as an empirical baseline, despite being the closest recent work addressing the same initialization limitations.

strengths: The core idea — clustering clients by full loss vectors rather than argmin-loss assignment (IFCA) or data-based similarity — is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained; the motivating Figure 1 example of IFCA failure is convincing.

The paper provides a genuine theoretical contribution for the linear regression setting: single-shot cluster recovery via a proximity condition (Thm A.9) and exponential convergence of the constructed models (Thm 4.2), with a nontrivial chain of concentration results.

Experimental coverage is broad: five datasets, supervised and unsupervised tasks, multiple skew types (label, feature, concept), a k-FED comparison in mixed linear regression, ablations (matching, clustering method, square-root loss), initialization robustness, and client-scaling experiments.
The method requires no near-optimal model initialization and applies to both supervised and unsupervised objectives, which is a practical advantage over several baselines.

The ablation isolating the bi-partite matching component, and the initialization-robustness comparison against IFCA (Fig. 2), directly support the paper's central claims about why CLoVE improves on IFCA.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. Iterating between (re)clustering clients and training cluster-specific models via FedAvg-style averaging is the standard CFL template (IFCA, FlexCFL, FeSEM, PACFL); the delta is using the full loss vector plus k-means as the clustering signal. The paper overstates the conceptual distance to prior work, and the empirical margins over FlexCFL/PACFL are small or absent in several settings (e.g., AG News accuracy, CIFAR-10 concept-shift accuracy, Amazon ARI where FlexCFL leads).

The theory is narrow and its assumptions are strong and somewhat at odds with the paper's narrative: analysis is restricted to mixed linear regression with Gaussian features, unit-norm, well-separated optima, small sigma, equal per-client sample sizes refreshed every round, K ≪ M, d, and balanced clusters. Theorem 4.1 requires either N = d near-orthogonal models or Δ-proximal models — so 'single-shot recovery' effectively still needs an initialization condition not far from IFCA-style separation, which undercuts the claimed robustness-to-initialization story as formally established (it is demonstrated empirically only).

Empirical rigor is limited: only 3 random seeds per configuration, no statistical significance testing for the many close comparisons, and the headline claim that CLoVE is 'the only algorithm that consistently ranks among the top performers' is weaker than the tables suggest (FedAvg wins Amazon Review; FlexCFL ties or wins several ARI/accuracy entries).

Reproducibility is incomplete: Table 6 links baselines' code but the CLoVE implementation itself is only 'self-implemented' with no stated code release, hyperparameter search protocol, or details on k-means initialization used in practice (the theory needs 'suitably initialized centers').

The key assumption that K is known a priori, and the privacy implications of clients shipping raw loss vectors (a K-dimensional summary of local data behavior) to the server, are discussed only in passing; the privacy paragraph is dismissive rather than an analysis.

Writing/presentation issues: repeated phrasing errors ('each of which each of which'), reliance on a Medium blog post [18] to support a quantitative ARI claim about k-means on MNIST, and the gap between the theoretical setup (square-root loss vectors) and the default experimental configuration (raw losses) is not clearly reconciled for the reader.

strengths: The core idea is simple and well-motivated: using full loss vectors (rather than single-model loss or gradients) as client embeddings for clustering in federated learning, which avoids the strict initialization requirements of IFCA and the data-distribution assumptions of k-FED-style methods. The motivating example in Figure 1 clearly illustrates why IFCA can fail.

The paper makes a reasonable effort to connect its method to theory: single-shot cluster recovery via k-means proximity conditions (building on Kumar–Kannan), and exponential convergence of the constructed models in a mixed linear regression setting. Lemma A.17 showing that IFCA's recovery condition implies loss-vector separation is a nice touch that sharpens the comparison with prior work.

Experiments are broad and fairly convincing: five datasets spanning supervised classification and unsupervised autoencoder reconstruction, four types of heterogeneity (label skews, feature shift, concept shift), a wide set of CFL and PFL baselines, ARI-based clustering evaluation, convergence speed analysis, robustness-to-initialization studies, and ablations (matching, clustering method, square-root loss). CLoVE is consistently at or near the top across settings, and the unsupervised results are a genuine differentiator from most CFL baselines.

The paper is generally well written and honest about aspects such as the privacy discussion (loss vectors sent to the server) and the cases where FedAvg remains competitive (Amazon Review), and it provides baseline source-code links, dataset/model details, and compute information, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The algorithm is essentially: cluster clients by k-means on loss vectors and re-match clusters to models each round. The individual ingredients (loss-based client assignment as in IFCA, iterative clustering as in CFL/FlexCFL, k-means on per-client statistics) are all established; the contribution is the specific combination and the robustness argument. This limits how exciting the contribution is for a main-track paper.

The theoretical guarantees rest on restrictive assumptions that limit their practical force: optimal models are unit-norm with separation Δ close to 1, noise σ ≪ 1, K ≪ d ≪ M, balanced clusters, freshly drawn i.i.d. data every round, and model collections that are either N = d ortho-normal or Δ-proximal with Δ-proximity already established. In practice N = K ≪ d, so the single-shot recovery result applies to the ortho-normal case only through an idealization. The claimed 'no near-optimal initialization needed' is thus only partially supported theoretically (the first round still requires the ortho-normal initialization analysis; Δ-proximal models are obtained only after round one).

The theory does not cover the deep learning settings where the method is most impressive; there is a gap between what is proved (linear regression, gradient averaging with fresh data each round) and what is demonstrated (non-convex models, persistent local datasets, Adam). The paper does not clearly flag this gap.

Communication and computational overhead of broadcasting all K models to all clients each round (a K× increase over FedAvg per round) is not analyzed or measured, which matters for the claimed real-world applicability.

The recently proposed improved loss-based method of Vardhan et al. [32], which the paper itself cites as addressing IFCA's initialization limitations, is discussed as motivation but not included as an experimental baseline — a notable omission given it is the closest competitor conceptually.

Experimental rigor is somewhat limited: only 3 random seeds, no significance testing, and several cells where CLoVE underperforms (e.g., CIFAR-10 under concept shift: 57.1 vs. FedAvg's 63.1; AG News where FlexCFL leads on accuracy) are not analyzed in depth.

Presentation has rough edges: repeated phrase in Section 3 ('each of which each of which'), reliance on a Medium blog post [18] for the MNIST k-means ARI claim, inconsistent naming ('Amazon News' vs. 'Amazon Review'), and typos in tables/captions. Typos like 'monotonicaly' and loosely stated matching-weights descriptions should be cleaned up.

The privacy treatment is minimal: sending raw loss vectors over all K models each round could itself leak information about a client's data beyond cluster membership; the paper's one-sentence dismissal is not a satisfactory treatment of this limitation for a federated-learning venue.

strengths: The proposed algorithm is simple, broadly applicable (supervised and unsupervised tasks), and well-motivated; the loss-vector perspective cleanly explains why it avoids IFCA's initialization trap (Fig. 1 is a compelling illustration).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: six datasets (image, text, reconstruction), many heterogeneity regimes (label/feature skew, concept shift), baselines spanning both CFL and generic PFL methods, ARI and convergence-speed metrics, plus ablations, partial participation, unknown-K, and scaling experiments in the appendix.

Theoretical treatment is non-trivial: the paper connects SLVs to the Kumar-Kannan proximity condition to obtain one-shot cluster recovery, and proves exponential convergence of models in the mixed linear regression setting; a comparison with IFCA's recovery condition (Lemma A.17) clarifies the relationship.
Strong emphasis on initialization robustness, with a dedicated experiment (Fig. 2) isolating initialization and first-round assignment effects versus IFCA.

Good reproducibility practices: hyperparameters, architectures, client counts, baseline source-code links, and compute details are reported; the authors state code will be released. Limitations and privacy implications are discussed honestly (Appendix C.2).
weaknesses: Limited originality: clustering clients by their loss/loss-vector profiles across multiple models is a natural incremental generalization of IFCA's per-model argmin assignment. The conceptual novelty beyond IFCA (k-means on the full loss vector instead of argmin) is modest.

Theory-practice gap on the central claim of 'eliminating near-optimal model initialization': the initialization-free guarantee (Theorem 4.1) relies on N = d ortho-normal models, i.e., a number of models equal to the parameter dimension, which is impractical; the practically relevant case (N = K models) requires the Δ-proximal condition, which is essentially the same near-optimal initialization assumption the paper criticizes in IFCA. Moreover, Theorem 4.1 needs 'suitably initialized' k-means centers. The paper's headline robustness claim is thus only partially supported by theory (though supported empirically).

Strong and somewhat unrealistic assumptions in the analysis: unit-norm optimal models with Δ ≈ 1, σ ≪ 1, each client resampling n_k i.i.d. points each round, K ≪ M, d, and the requirement dK^4 polylog(M) = o(nM). Generalization to non-linear models or non-i.i.d. client data is not addressed.

Accuracy results are not uniformly state-of-the-art: FedAvg beats CLoVE on Amazon (99.0 vs 86.8) and FlexCFL beats it on AG News and some label-skew settings (Tables 1, 7). The abstract's 'state-of-the-art model accuracy' claim is somewhat overstated; 'consistently near the top' would be more accurate. This is acknowledged in the text but not in the abstract/intro.

Computational overhead of evaluating all K̂ models on every client every round (before stability) is discussed only qualitatively; no measured wall-clock/FLOP comparison against baselines is provided despite the claim of 'substantially lower' overhead than IFCA/CFL-S.

The unknown-K mechanism (silhouette-score selection over K ≤ K̂, with K̂ = 2× a one-shot clustering method from FlexCFL/PACFL) is heuristic and somewhat circular, since it depends on those one-shot methods working reasonably.
Evidence for the motivating claim that k-means on MNIST achieves ~50% ARI rests on a Medium blog post citation (Treder-Tschechlov, 2024), which is a weak source for a load-bearing motivating claim.

Experiments use small CNNs/MLPs/autoencoders, few seeds (3), and moderate client counts in the main results; the code link in the manuscript appears as dangling text ('can be found here:'), which should be fixed or clarified (presumably anonymization).

strengths: The proposed algorithm (Alg. 1) is simple and well-specified: clustering clients by k-means on loss vectors across multiple models, min-cost bipartite matching to models, and per-cluster aggregation. Its applicability to unsupervised settings (autoencoders, Table 4, Fig. 5) is a genuine practical advantage over several baselines and, to my knowledge, an underexplored evaluation regime for CFL.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: six datasets, ten baselines spanning CFL and general PFL, multiple heterogeneity regimes (label skews 1-4, feature skew, concept shift), plus ablations (Table 17-18), partial participation (Table 14, Fig. 4), unknown K (Table 12), early stopping (Table 13), and scaling to 1000 clients (Tables 15-16). Table 3 shows a convincing speed advantage (ARI >= 0.9 within 2-3 rounds) over all baselines.

The theoretical section is structured around a recognized technique (the Kumar-Kannan proximity condition) and includes concentration analysis for square-root loss vectors (Lemmas A.1-A.9), exponential model convergence (Theorem 4.2), and a comparison lemma showing IFCA's recovery condition implies loss-vector separation (Lemma A.17).
Code for self-implemented baselines is provided, and baseline sources are linked (Table 6); experimental details (Table 5, Appendix D) are sufficiently specific to support reproduction.
weaknesses: A gap exists between the theory and the algorithm actually evaluated. The analysis covers square-root loss vectors (SLVs) with Remark A.12 admitting that for plain loss vectors 'the analysis gets more complex and we therefore leave that for future work,' yet the main experiments appear to use raw losses (the ablation in Table 17 finds square-root loss makes 'no significant change'). Theorem 4.1 also requires 'suitably initialized centers' for k-means, which partially undercuts the headline claim that CLoVE 'eliminates the need for near-optimal model initialization' and 'ensures optimal cluster recovery with high probability' relative to IFCA.

The theory's scope is narrow: mixed linear regression with unit-norm, well-separated optima (Delta close to 1), equal data counts nk per client, low noise (sigma << 1), known K, and specific participation/learning-rate conditions (Assumption A.15, Lemma A.13). These assumptions do not plausibly hold for the CNN/autoencoder experiments that carry the paper's empirical claims, so the theoretical results validate feasibility in one linear regime rather than explain the broad empirical success.

Novelty is modest. Clustering clients by their loss profile across models is a natural incremental step beyond IFCA (which uses argmin loss) and beyond multi-model variants; the paper's positioning that this 'avoids the local optima issues' of EM approaches is asserted more strongly than the limited linear-regression analysis supports.

Several claims are weakly supported. The motivation cites an ARI of ~50% for k-means on MNIST from a Medium blog post (Treder-Tschechlov, 2024), an inappropriate citation for a technical premise. The claim to be 'the first to propose an algorithm that can cluster correctly using autoencoders in a fully unsupervised setting' (Appendix D) is asserted without citation or qualification.

Text-classification results are mixed: FedAvg substantially outperforms CLoVE on Amazon Reviews (99.0 vs 86.8) and FlexCFL leads on AG News (60.2 vs 55.1, Table 1), which the narrative of 'state-of-the-art accuracy across a variety of tasks' glosses over; the offered explanations are plausible but qualitative.

Results are based on only 3 random seeds, and some reported variances are large (e.g., CFL-S 82.5 +/- 21.8; IFCA CIFAR-10 85.7 +/- 6.5), making fine-grained rankings uncertain. Also, the code availability statements ('can be found here:', 'can be found at', pp. 6, 27) appear to be incomplete placeholders in this version, which hampers reproducibility verification.

Privacy treatment is thin: CLoVE transmits per-client loss vectors to the server, which is strictly more information than FedAvg's weight updates; Appendix C.2 acknowledges the leakage implications 'remain underexplored.' Given that privacy preservation is cited as a core motivation of FL in the introduction, a more rigorous treatment or at least a clearer limitation statement would be appropriate.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated algorithm: clustering clients by loss vectors evaluated across multiple models is a natural and clean extension of IFCA-style loss-based approaches, and Fig. 1 gives a clear intuitive account of why it avoids IFCA's failure mode of collapsing all clients into one cluster.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper compares against a broad set of CFL (CFL-S, IFCA, FlexCFL, FeSEM, PACFL) and generic PFL (Per-FedAvg, FedProto, FedALA, FedPAC) baselines across six datasets, multiple heterogeneity regimes (label skew, feature skew, concept shift), and reports both accuracy and clustering quality (ARI) with convergence speed (Tables 1-3), which is the kind of evaluation the CFL area needs.

Strong ablation and robustness analysis: the initialization experiments (Fig. 2), partial participation (Table 14), unknown-K setting (Table 12), early stopping (Table 13), scaling (Tables 15-16), and component ablations (Tables 17-18) substantiate the practical claims of robustness to poor initialization and low communication overhead.

A nontrivial theoretical contribution: Theorems 4.1/4.2 establish single-shot cluster recovery via the Kumar-Kannan proximity condition and exponential convergence of models to optima in a mixed linear regression setting, with complete proofs in Appendix A.

The unsupervised/autoencoder evaluation (Tables 4, 16; Figs. 5-6) addresses an understudied setting, and the paper claims with justification to be the first extensive CFL evaluation in the unsupervised setting.
Code and detailed experimental setup (Tables 5-6) are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: A gap between the central 'no near-optimal initialization needed' claim and the theory: Theorem 4.1 requires the model collection to be either ortho-normal (N = d randomly drawn unit vectors) or ∆-proximal (each model within ∆/4 of its optimum). ∆-proximal initialization is essentially the IFCA-style assumption the paper criticizes, and the ortho-normal case is a special construction that is hard to interpret for general deep models. The empirical robustness (Fig. 2) is convincing, but the theory does not actually prove initialization-agnostic recovery in the general setting.

The theoretical assumptions are restrictive beyond initialization: σ ≪ 1, unit-norm optima with ∆ close to 1, identical nk per client with fresh i.i.d. data each round, K fixed and known a priori, and 'suitably initialized' k-means centers. The theorem probabilities (1 − δ − 1/polylog(M)) and conditions like dK^4 polylog(M) = o(nM) make the guarantees weaker than the abstract's phrasing ('recovers clusters accurately with high probability in a single round') suggests. The paper should soften or qualify these claims.

Moderate novelty: the core mechanism (use losses on cluster models to decide assignment) is inherited from IFCA; the contribution is aggregating losses across all K models into an embedding and clustering those, plus bipartite matching. This is a sensible refinement rather than a fundamentally new technique, and the paper would benefit from a more precise delineation against IFCA's analysis.

Theory covers only linear regression, while the main experiments are deep networks; there is no theoretical or semi-synthetic evidence connecting the assumptions to the deep-learning regime where the claims of robustness are made.

Some baseline results raise tuning concerns: FeSEM's near-zero accuracies (e.g., 11.2% on CIFAR-10) and CFL-S's huge variance (82.5 ± 21.8) suggest possible misconfiguration; IFCA and CLoVE are self-implemented while others use third-party code, so fairness of comparison is partly unverifiable. Only 3 seeds are used.

In several settings CLoVE does not win (Amazon Reviews where FedAvg dominates, AG News where FlexCFL wins, label skews 3/4 in Appendix E.1.2 where FedAvg is best); the paper discusses this honestly, but the abstract's 'state-of-the-art model accuracy' claim is somewhat stronger than the mixed results warrant.

The link to the authors' code appears empty in the manuscript ('can be found here:' / 'can be found at' with no URL), which weakens the reproducibility claim as submitted; this should be fixed or replaced by an anonymized repository.

There is no consolidated limitations section; caveats are scattered (Appendix C on privacy admits leakage questions are underexplored, Remark A.12 admits the LV analysis is incomplete). A dedicated discussion of when CLoVE could fail (e.g., clients whose loss vectors are genuinely similar, adversarial clients, very heterogeneous cluster sizes) would strengthen the paper.
